newsitem.title: USA: Clinton allies predict death of Whitewater probe.
newsitem.headline: Clinton allies predict death of Whitewater probe.

text.p: President Bill Clinton's home state allies gleefully predicted a quick end to the Whitewater investigation on Tuesday after lead prosecutor Kenneth Starr said he planned to resign by this summer.

Although Starr said his decision to step down to become dean of a law school did not mean the probe into Clinton's personal and political finances was over, his Arkansas critics quickly interpreted the move as a sign the worst had passed.

"Turn out the lights, the party's over," said Dan Guthrie, attorney for an Arkansas banker who was indicted by Starr but was acquitted on charges he illegally converted bank funds into contributions for Clinton's political campaigns. "An independent counsel is not going to walk away from a case like this if anything else significant is going to happen."
Starr, 50, said on Monday he will step aside to become dean of the Pepperdine University law school by Aug. 1 but he cautioned against speculation that the investigation might be at a dead end.

"We have many able and competent professionals both in Little Rock and Washington who are very familiar with the investigation. The office will be, I am sure, in very good hands," Starr told reporters.
Saying the probe "is at a very active point" and a lot could still happen between now and August, he continued to work at his Little Rock office on Tuesday.

But local analysts said Starr's resignation indicated the investigation had lost some of its earlier momentum. "If I were Clinton I'd be somewhat encouraged," said University of Arkansas political science professor Cal Ledbetter Jr.

In recent months, the Arkansas phase of Starr's probe is believed to have focused on first lady Hillary Rodham Clinton. Prosecutors are trying to determine whether she performed legal work for an Arkansas real estate project that was illegally funded and whether she was part of an alleged conspiracy to conceal details of the deal.

Since taking over as special prosecutor in 1994, Starr has won convictions against James and Susan McDougal, who were former partners of the Clintons in the Whitewater real estate venture, as well as former Arkansas Gov. Jim Guy Tucker.

Former U.S. Associate Attorney General Webster Hubbell, at one time a law partner of Hillary Clinton, and Steve Smith, an aide to Clinton when he was Arkansas governor, pleaded guilty to charges brought by Starr's team.

Clinton testified for the defence in the trial of Tucker and the McDougals, denying allegations that he pressured an Arkansas banker to extend an illegal $300,000 loan. But James McDougal is cooperating with Starr as part of a plea bargain and has reportedly recanted his trial testimony.

Starr appeared to be closing in on the Clintons after winning convictions against the McDougals but he suffered a setback last August when two bankers who were political allies of Clinton were acquitted of fraud and conspiracy charges.

Gene Lyons, a Little Rock writer who has published a book attacking the Whitewater investigation as the product of partisan politics, said he believed Starr was quitting because he had no firm evidence against the Clintons. "I think maybe Starr has come to his senses ... It looks like he has sized it up and decided he doesn't want to go down with the ship."
